narrative:
The 2018 Detroit Tigers entered the season as a franchise in transition, a once-proud dynasty now stripped of its star power and tasked with absorbing a painful rebuilding process. The opening series offered a fleeting glimpse of possibility — Dixon Machado's two-run double on Opening Day electrified the small faithful crowd — but Gregory Polanco's three-run blast off Alex Wilson the same night foreshadowed the relief-pitching nightmares that would haunt Detroit all year. The Tigers finished March 0-1 and stumbled through April at 11-15, too often undone in the late innings by a bullpen that couldn't hold leads.

May brought the closest thing to hope Detroit could manufacture. The team played .500 ball at 15-14, fueled by young contributors like JaCoby Jones and an offense that occasionally caught fire behind Nick Castellanos and a fading but still dangerous Victor Martinez. But even within that competent month, the bullpen was a recurring villain — Shane Greene surrendering a lead-erasing homer to Seattle's Mitch Haniger in late May was a microcosm of the fragility underneath the surface.

June marked the true collapse. The Tigers went 10-18 as the bullpen imploded with alarming regularity. Greene was torched multiple times in crucial spots, Warwick Saupold served up a grand slam to the Twins' Ehire Adrianza, and the losses piled up in demoralizing fashion. July and August were more of the same — a 10-14 July and a catastrophic 8-19 August that ended any pretense of competitiveness. The single-game nadir may have been August 31, when Gleyber Torres' walk-off single off Alex Wilson in New York sent three Yankees home with a gut-punch loss worth over half a win probability in one swing.

September became a showcase for the organization's future. Jeimer Candelario homered twice in meaningful spots, Niko Goodrum demonstrated his versatility and pop, and the ageless Victor Martinez provided dignity in his final days as a Tiger. James Adduci's three-run homer on September 16 gave the dwindling fanbase something to cheer. The 2018 Tigers finished 64-98, outscored by 166 runs, a team that suffered more than it celebrated — but one that planted seeds in younger players who would define whatever came next in Detroit.

chapters.title: Opening Day Whiplash
chapters.description: The Tigers open with a dramatic swing of emotions on Opening Day, rising on Machado's clutch double before the bullpen surrenders a pivotal three-run homer.

chapters.title: Sparks of Life in April
chapters.description: John Hicks, Dixon Machado, and JaCoby Jones deliver highlight-reel moments that keep April afloat, even as the bullpen continues to bleed leads.

chapters.title: Treading Water in May
chapters.description: Detroit plays .500 ball behind timely hits from Castellanos and Iglesias, but the bullpen keeps finding new ways to squander close games.

chapters.title: June Collapse
chapters.description: A brutal 10-18 June exposes the team's fatal flaws as Shane Greene and the relief corps serve up crusher after crusher in high-leverage situations.

chapters.title: Summer Slide
chapters.description: July and August bring mounting losses and a devastating late-game collapse against the Yankees that crystallizes just how far Detroit has fallen.

chapters.title: September Auditions
chapters.description: With the season lost, Candelario, Goodrum, and Martinez offer glimpses of the future and past in a meaningless but emotionally rich final stretch.
